title: What I like — and what I don't
goal: Say what you like and dislike with the gustatzen zait pattern, talk about hobbies, and invite other people.
bekal: use *zait, zaizu, zaio, zaigu, zaizue, zaie* and the plural form *zaizkit*
use the ending *-ekin* ("with") and give your opinion

dialogs.title: Elkarrizketa — Zer gustatzen zaizu?
dialogs.intro: In the euskaltegi cafeteria, Nerea sits across from Budi and plays a song on her phone.

lines.speaker: Nerea:
lines.id: Budi, what music do you like?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Rock musika gustatzen zait. Eta zuri?
lines.id: I like rock music. What about you?
lines.literal: rock music pleasing to-me-it. and to-you?

lines.speaker: Nerea:
lines.text: Euskal kantu inprobisatuak dira. Oso zailak dira!
lines.id: They're improvised Basque songs. They're really hard!
lines.literal: Basque song improvised-the(pl) are. very hard-the(pl) are!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Interesting! Do you like sports too?

lines.speaker: Nerea:
lines.text: Bai, asko. Igandeetan mendira joaten naiz lagunekin.
lines.id: Yes, a lot. On Sundays I go to the mountains with friends.
lines.literal: yes, much. Sunday-pl-in mountain-to going am friend-pl-with.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Niri ere mendia gustatzen zait, baina goizegi da niretzat!
lines.id: I like the mountains too, but it's too early for me!
lines.literal: to-me also mountain-the pleasing to-me-it, but early-too is me-for!

lines.speaker: Nerea:
lines.text: Ha, ha! Eta futbola? Athletic gustatzen zaizu?
lines.id: Ha, ha! And soccer? Do you like Athletic?
lines.literal: ha, ha! and soccer-the? Athletic pleasing to-you-it?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Yes, I really like watching their games.

lines.speaker: Nerea:
lines.text: Orduan larunbatean San Mamesera goaz, ados?
lines.id: Then on Saturday we're going to San Mamés, OK?
lines.literal: then Saturday-on San Mamés-to we-go, agreed?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Yes, of course! I'm so happy.

notes: **The thing you like is the doer; you're just the receiver.** English says "I like music": I'm the subject, music is the object. Basque says *musika gustatzen zait* — "music is pleasing to me". The music does the work; you're only the one it affects. Spanish (*me gusta*) and Italian do the same.

**If you like several things, the auxiliary goes plural too.** *Partidak gustatzen **zaizkit*** (I like those games), not *zait*. Notice the inserted *-zki-* that marks the plural. This is the most common A1 mistake, and the easiest to fix: look at the end of the noun — if it has *-ak*, use *zaizkit*.

**Niri, zuri — the receiver is marked with -ri.** You can say it for emphasis: *Niri bertsolaritza gustatzen zait* ("as for **me**, I like bertsolaritza"). Without emphasis, the auxiliary alone is enough — *zait* already means "to me".

**Bertsolaritza — improvised sung verse.** A *bertsolari* is given a topic and a rhythm, then has to sing a rhyming verse on the spot, with no preparation. The championship final fills an indoor arena with over ten thousand people. If you want to understand why this language has survived two thousand years, watch one bertso — even before you understand the words.

blocks.text: The formula: **thing you like + gustatzen + auxiliary for to whom**. The thing you like takes the ordinary article (*-a* or *-ak*), with no doer's hat.

head: Euskara
English
rows: I don't like it at all.
I hate it. (ordinary pattern, with the doer's hat)
It's all the same to me.

blocks.title: Other verbs that work like gustatu
items: *iruditu* — seem: *Zaila iruditzen zait.* (it seems hard to me)
*ahaztu* — slip one's mind: *Ahaztu zait!* (I forgot — literally "it slipped my mind")
*gertatu* — happen: *Zer gertatzen zaizu?* (what's wrong with you?)
In all these sentences you're not the doer but the one affected. Basque sees feelings as something that **happens to** people, not something people do.

head: Euskara
English
rows: rural sports: stone lifting, log sawing, tug-of-war
soccer — Athletic Club in Bilbo, Real Sociedad in Donostia

blocks.text: *Athletic Club* has a habit that's unique in the world: it only fields players born or raised in Euskal Herria. The rule has lasted more than a century, and it explains why a match at San Mamés stadium feels more like a giant village festival than a sports event.

blocks.title: Inviting and answering invitations
items: *Zinemara joan nahi duzu?* — Do you want to go to the movies?
*Bai, noski!* / *Bai, primeran!* — Yes, of course! / Yes, great!
*Ezin dut, sentitzen dut.* — I can't, sorry.

blocks.text: Don't mix this up with the *-z* you learned in Unit 9: *-ekin* is for the **person** who comes along (*lagunekin*), *-z* is for the **means** you use (*autobusez*). English uses "with" and "by" — Basque keeps them apart in the same way.

blocks.title: Giving your opinion
items: *Uste dut baietz / ezetz.* — I think so / I don't think so.
*Interesgarria da.* — It's interesting. *Aspergarria da.* — It's boring.
*Zoragarria da!* — It's wonderful! *Izugarria da.* — It's terrible.
*Bat nator zurekin.* — I agree with you.
It's all the same to me.
